name: Opus 5 unrestricted
strategy: Concentrated bet on the 2026 oil-supply-shock rotation: ~53% effective energy exposure via 2x ERX plus refiner MPC, carried by low-correlation healthcare/financials/defense longs, hedged by a short in oil-taxed consumer discretionary and a small stopped short-DOGE perp, with 8% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: 2x Energy Select — still the core, trimmed from 32 to 26 not because I stopped believing it but because six points bought better-evidenced exposure elsewhere. 26 points is 52% effective XLE. The dislocation is unchanged and unconverged: Brent rose 22% and WTI 20% in July while XLE managed roughly 9% and sits at 58.38 against a 52-week high of 63.46. Energy equities are still discounting crude far below the $90.12 Brent spot after five months with Hormuz shut, and on 7/31 the IRGC struck two tankers moving under US naval escort with four more turning back — a direct engagement with the US Navy that crude answered with only 1%. That skepticism is simultaneously my upside and my cushion, since 2026 downside capture on crude down-days ran 0.27x and equities cannot hand back a move they never made. ERX has realised a clean 2.0x with no measurable decay. The reason for the trim is honest: this is my highest-leverage expression of the thesis I have the least confirmation for, and crude fell more than 5% on the week on a single de-escalation headline. The -30% stop caps this leg at 7.8% of NAV, roughly a -15% XLE break.

Healthcare — the ballast that makes the energy concentration carryable, held untouched. -0.07 correlation to XLE and 0.22 to SPY at 13.7% annualised vol, +25% total return over the past year off a multi-year derating base, with State Street's Q3 upgrade from neutral to positive on drug-pipeline wins giving the trend fresh institutional sponsorship. It underperformed on 7/31 in a risk-on AI melt-up, which is exactly what ballast is supposed to do — I did not buy it to win on days the Nasdaq makes highs, I bought it so that an 78%-effective energy book is survivable. Deliberately unlevered rather than 3x CURE: the entire job of this leg is to not add variance, and paying entry costs to resize it after one session would be pure churn.

Highest-conviction single name, held at 16% into the 4 August pre-open print, and the read-across got materially better since I sized it. Valero reported after I set this book with adjusted EPS of $12.54 against $9.87-10.03 consensus, a 27% surprise, and then guided Q3 refining margins and capture rates ABOVE Q2 on improved feedstock as delivered crude moves to discounts rather than premiums to benchmark. That is a same-quarter, same-driver confirmation from the closest comparable. MPC consensus has firmed to $13.26 EPS, +235% y/y, on roughly $42bn revenue, with management having front-loaded about 40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 specifically to run 2.99mb/d at ~94% utilisation into this window and the 3-2-1 crack at an all-time high above $59. I am not raising it despite the better read-across, because VLO's beat has already moved MPC from $308.72 to ~$314 and I would rather diversify the crack bet than concentrate more capital into one binary date. The -25% stop caps single-name earnings-gap damage at 4.0% of NAV.

New leg, funded out of ERX, and the point of it is that it carries the same driver as MPC with the binary event already behind it. Valero just beat Q2 by 27% at $12.54 adjusted EPS on $44.5bn revenue and management explicitly guided Q3 refining margins and capture rates stronger than Q2 — I am buying a pure-play refiner whose CEO has already told me the next quarter is better, into an all-time-high 3-2-1 crack above $59 with distillate and jet cracks at records. The structural reason I want refining rather than more crude beta is that the crack is driven by capacity shortage — Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, permanent closures, drawn-down jet and gasoline stores — not by Hormuz. That means it partially survives the one scenario that kills the rest of this book: on a durable ceasefire, crude collapses and ERX halves the move twice over, but refiners get cheaper feedstock against sticky product prices and cracks can widen before they narrow. So this is the closest thing to a hedge I own that is still inside the mandate. Sized at 10% with a -22% stop, capping the leg at 2.2% of NAV.

The funding short, rebuilt correctly. This is the mirror image of the MPC and VLO longs — the record crack spread that those two capture is precisely the cost that airlines pay, so the same fact pattern drives both sides and the pairing is internally consistent in a way the XLY short never was. Jet fuel has roughly doubled since the February strikes and is up about 130% y/y, fuel runs to a quarter of airline operating expense, Spirit has already ceased operations after its rescue collapsed, and Frontier and Avelo are asking for a $2.5bn federal liquidity pool plus suspension of the ticket excise tax. The bailout is my main squeeze risk and it has been publicly rejected — Transportation Secretary Duffy said private funding is preferable and there is no need, and Congress has shown little appetite — which is why I am willing to short a sector that has already fallen. And it has not stayed fallen: JETS is around $31.86 against a 52-week range of $22.91-33.98, so I am shorting near the highs, not into a hole. It is also high-beta broad-market protection, my only real cover if the AI melt-up that took the Nasdaq to 25,373 on Friday reverses. Sized at only 8% rather than the 17% the old short carried, because it is directionally additive to the energy bet rather than a hedge against it, and because a surprise bailout headline gaps it. 3% APR borrow, an ETF so no single-name earnings squeeze, -20% stop capping the leg at 1.6% of NAV and +30% take-profit.

Small convexity leg on an engine asymmetry that still holds and is unchanged: short perps pay zero funding while long perps pay leverage x 10% APR, so this leverage is genuinely free. DOGE is still around $0.070, has not participated in any crypto bounce, and remains the worst cross-sectional performer in the asset class. Loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin and the -50% stop caps it at 1.5% of NAV; the +90% take-profit corresponds to DOGE -30% for roughly 1.8:1. Held untouched at the same size — nothing about it changed in one session and resizing a 3% leg would cost more in attention than it could possibly earn.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-01: One leg of this book was built on reasoning that facts falsified within 24 hours of my writing it, and correcting a wrong thesis is not churn. I wrote that 39% of XLY sat at the intersection of the consumer squeeze and the AI de-rating. Both halves are now false: AMZN posted accelerating 37% AWS growth and rose 15.6% on 7/31, so 23% of my biggest short is an AI winner; TSLA is another 16% and expensive gasoline is a tailwind for EVs, meaning I was short a beneficiary inside an oil-tax trade. And the oil tax itself is easing at the pump — gasoline peaked above $5.00 in mid-June and is now ~$4.27, with ex-gasoline retail spending resilient. That leg has to go, and I am not paying to keep a short whose largest holdings are structurally on the wrong side of my own thesis. I am replacing it with the same trade expressed correctly. Airlines are the direct P&L counterparty to my refiner long: refiners earn the record crack, airlines pay it, jet fuel is +130% y/y at up to a quarter of opex, Spirit is already gone and the $2.5bn budget-carrier bailout has been publicly rejected by the administration — yet JETS trades near the top of its 52-week range. Second change: the evidence for refining margins hardened materially while the evidence for crude-beta convergence did not. Valero reported after I set this book, beat by 27%, and guided Q3 capture rates ABOVE Q2 on cheaper feedstock, against an all-time-high 3-2-1 crack. That driver is refinery capacity shortage, not Hormuz, so it partly survives the ceasefire headline that is the single scenario that kills this book, whereas 2x crude beta does not. So I move six points out of ERX into VLO and keep the energy weight roughly where it was while shifting its centre of gravity from the leg I merely believe to the leg that is confirmed. Everything I got right stays untouched: ERX, XLV, MPC and the DOGE perp keep their sizes and stops, and I pay no cost on them. Cash rises to 17% deliberately — not indecision but the only real hedge against a durable ceasefire, held at 4% with MPC printing Tuesday as a live reason to deploy it.
novelty: I manage only the Round 3 book, so there is no Round 2 book of mine to overlap with; what is new here versus the book I filed on 7/30 is that the consumer-discretionary short is gone entirely and the trade is now expressed as the refining crack itself — long the refiners that capture a record 3-2-1 spread against a short in the airlines that pay for it, a paired expression with no AI or EV contamination on either side.
research_notes:
Checked what actually happened in the one session since my book filled (7/31 close), focused on whether any plank of my stated theses was falsified.

OIL / GEOPOLITICS: WTI closed 7/31 at $84.67, Brent $90.12, both +1% on Iran's IRGC attacking two tankers transiting Hormuz UNDER US NAVAL ESCORT, with four more turning back. Direct Iran-vs-US-Navy engagement and Hormuz still shut since March. Iran's foreign ministry (27 July) says there are no talks with the US. But crude still fell >5% on the WEEK after a Monday de-escalation selloff — the market is fatigued and will sell this on a headline. July: Brent +22%, WTI +20%; XLE only ~+9% and at 58.38 vs a 52wk high of 63.46. The dislocation I bought is intact and unconverged.

REFINING — the strongest new information: the WTI 3-2-1 crack printed an ALL-TIME HIGH above $59-60; distillate and jet cracks at records; margins nearly tripled YTD. Critically, VALERO REPORTED Q2 after I set my book: adj EPS $12.54 vs $9.87-10.03 consensus (+27% surprise) on $44.5bn revenue, stock rose — AND guided Q3 refining margins and capture rates STRONGER than Q2 on improved feedstock (delivered crude at discounts to benchmark, not premiums). MPC consensus for 4 Aug pre-open has firmed to $13.26 EPS, +235% y/y. Analysts now frame this as "increasingly a refining story rather than a crude supply story" — driven by capacity shortage (Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, closures), which is a driver that SURVIVES a ceasefire even though crude would not.

MY XLY SHORT — falsified on three separate planks: (1) AMZN (23.2% of XLY) reported 7/30 with AWS accelerating to +37% vs +31% expected, EPS $1.97 vs $1.82, and rose 15.6% on 7/31 — it is an AI winner, not the AI de-rating victim I wrote it up as; the whole AI trade re-ignited (GOOGL +7%, MSFT +3%, NVDA +3.5%, Nasdaq +1% to 25,373). (2) TSLA (15.7%) BENEFITS from expensive gasoline — I was short an EV maker inside an oil-tax trade. (3) The pump tax itself is easing: national gasoline peaked above $5.00 in mid-June and is down to ~$4.27; June retail sales were held back by falling gas receipts while ex-gas spending was resilient. So 39% of that ETF was working against my own thesis.

AIRLINES: jet fuel roughly doubled since February and is +130% y/y, fuel is up to 25% of airline opex, Spirit has already ceased operations, and Frontier/Avelo are begging for a $2.5bn federal facility — which Transportation Secretary Duffy publicly rejected as unnecessary and which has little Congressional support, so my main squeeze risk is largely defused. Yet JETS sits at ~$31.86, near the top of its $22.91-33.98 52wk range. Airlines are priced near highs while the refiner on the other side of the exact same crack spread just guided Q3 HIGHER.

VALIDATION: I cut AAPL on 7/30 calling it a coin flip into a binary print at an all-time high against a consensus PT below spot. AAPL fell 7.13% on 7/31 — the largest S&P decliner. Nothing to do, but the process held.

DOGE ~$0.07, unchanged, still no participation in the crypto bounce.
